title: Adaptive priority lane surge scratchpad
content:
Context:
Personal lab notes for a quick exploration of priority lanes + adaptive admission during short, high-intensity ingress spikes. Want to capture setup, raw results, oddities, and concrete next actions. Keep this informal — iterative log.

Hypothesis:
- Priority lanes (fast-path for high-tier tokens) + adaptive admission (reject/backoff based on instant qps) will reduce p99 of high-priority requests during microbursts without catastrophically hurting lower-priority throughput.
- Warm KV-cache interactions: priming high-priority lane first should amplify benefits; cold-cache spikes may dominate cost.

Environment:
- Fleet: 4x A100-80GB (dedicated pool) behind ingress routing sim.
- Runtime: redwood-inference-runtime v0.76 (local dev build with microbatching fix)
- Model: redwood-mini-6b-8bit (seq len 512 test configuration)
- Orchestration: local k8s single-az, autoscaler disabled for these runs
- Observability: per-request traces + tesla-agent GPU util / cgroup metrics, bucketed into 1s windows

Traffic patterns and scenarios:
1) Poisson baseline: 150 qps lambda, 10% high-priority (HP). 20m run.
2) Microburst: steady 100 qps, then 600 qps spike for 30s, HP fraction ramps 10% -> 40% during spike.
3) Stair-step multi-burst: three spikes (60s each) with 3x tiers of HP concentration.
4) Cold-cache variant: flush KV-cache across nodes immediately before spike.

Admission policies tested (A/B matrix):
A: FIFO (no lanes), simple queue cap=200
B: Static priority lanes (HP lane weight 0.6), queue cap HP=120, LP=80
C: Adaptive admission - measured instant qps + tail latency feedback, drops LP first when GPU util > 78% or p95(HP) > 250ms
D: Adaptive w/ preemptive KV-priming: preferentially dispatch HP requests to warmed shards during spike window

Key runtime knobs recorded: concurrency target (1,2,4), microbatch window (10ms / 50ms), max_batch_tokens (2048 / 4096).

Raw snapshot (selected) - microburst scenario, 30s spike, cold-cache:
- A (FIFO): p50=120ms, p90=340ms, p95=490ms, p99=1.4s, throughput during spike ~ 520 qps accepted, GPU util spiky 35->95%
- B (Static lanes): p50(HP)=110ms, p90(HP)=280ms, p99(HP)=950ms; p99(LP)=1.6s; overall accepted qps ~ 510 (LP starved)
- C (Adaptive): p50(HP)=105ms, p90(HP)=220ms, p99(HP)=420ms; LP p99 bumped to 2.1s but many LP requests dropped (5% drop) to keep HP SLOs; accepted qps ~ 480 (with ~7% drops across both tiers)
- D (Adaptive + priming): p50(HP)=98ms, p90(HP)=190ms, p99(HP)=360ms; drop rate 2% LP; throughput accepted ~ 495; GPU util smoother, fewer tail spikes

Small ASCII p99 over time (D run, 60s window, numbers in ms):
Time(s) | p99(HP)
0-10    | 120  135  140  150  160  170  180  190  200  210
10-20   | 220  230  240  260  280  300  340  360  350  330
20-30   | 310  300  280  260  240  220  210  200  195  190
(rough - each value is 1s bucket)

Observations / oddities:
- Cold KV-cache dominated first 8s of spike; priming reduced that tail significantly. Even with identical accepted qps, warmed shards drop p99 by ~2x in first 10s.
- Adaptive policy can be tuned aggressively to protect HP SLOs with modest global drop rates (~3–7%). We observed diminishing returns when using microbatch window >20ms (adds 30–50ms to p50).
- Preemptive priming requires a fast shard map; slight staleness (200ms) can cause misrouting and transient 5–10% extra latency on HP. Need to quantify map staleness tolerance.
- When GPU util oscillates quickly, admission decisions chase the metric and cause small oscillations in accepted qps. Adding 1s exponential smoothing to util input stabilizes behavior.

Quick cost/efficiency note:
- Static lanes improved HP metrics but effectively reduced total accepted throughput (LP starvation). Adaptive approach preserved more overall throughput at the expense of some LP drops — net token-per-second accepted across fleet was ~95% of FIFO but with HP p99 improved by ~2–3x.

Immediate next steps (actionable):
- Re-run D with varying shard-map staleness knobs (0ms, 50ms, 200ms) and capture misroute rate and HP p99. (JIRA-INF-8421)
- Add a short test to simulate very short microbursts (10s) to see if priming overhead is worth it for brief spikes.
- Build lightweight synthetic priming: sample small prefixes from live workload and precompute KV blocks for top-20 tokens.
- Surface a dashboard: per-lane drop rate, p99, and priming hit-rate (1s granularity).

Notes to self / heuristics:
- If expected spike < 15s, priming might not pay unless KV warmup latency > 200ms for first tokens.
- Prefer smoothing on GPU util; avoid reacting to single 1s buckets.
- Default microbatch window to 10ms for latency-sensitive HP lane; allow LP lane to use 50ms to optimize throughput.

Random loose thoughts (for later):
- Could use probabilistic admission rather than hard drops for LP, tuned by real-time gradient descent on p95(target)-observed.
- Consider hybrid: reserve small always-on capacity for HP (like 10% of nodes) during predictable spike windows (calendar-based).

References & quick links:
- Load generator config: git://perfgen/configs/mika/priority-lane.json
- Notebook: https://notebooks.internal.redwood.ai/mika/priority-lane-analysis.ipynb

2026-02-14 09:55 UTC - ran microburst cold-cache (A,B,C,D) - collected traces
2026-02-14 10:40 UTC - initial parsing & small table above
2026-02-20 16:03 UTC - added priming variant (D) and re-ran; much better first-10s tail

End of scratchpad. Will extract a short one-pager for the team if results hold on more runs.
